title: The $38 Billion Ceiling and the $300 Million Floor: How Two Deals Are Redrawing the Economics of Artificial Intelligence
excerpt: OpenAI caps Microsoft’s revenue share while Salesforce prepares to spend more on Anthropic tokens than it does on engineering salaries — and Indian tech workers are caught in the crossfire
body:
Two announcements in the past week have done more to clarify the business model of artificial intelligence than a year’s worth of product launches. Together, they describe a world in which the companies that build AI models and the companies that consume them are renegotiating the terms of their dependency — and the engineers who once sat between them are being written out of the equation.

**The cap: OpenAI and Microsoft**

OpenAI and Microsoft have agreed to cap Microsoft’s cumulative revenue share at $38 billion through 2030. Under the original partnership, Microsoft was entitled to a growing slice of OpenAI’s revenue in perpetuity — a deal struck when OpenAI was a research lab burning cash and Microsoft was its lifeline. That arrangement no longer reflects reality. OpenAI is now reportedly valued at $852 billion and is preparing an IPO. The cap effectively buys OpenAI’s freedom.

In exchange, Microsoft retains a non-exclusive licence to OpenAI’s models through 2032 and unlocks an estimated $6 billion in accelerated 2026 cash flows. The exclusivity clause — which prevented OpenAI from selling to rival cloud platforms — has been dropped entirely. OpenAI is now free to sell capacity to Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud, clearing a legal hurdle for its reported $50 billion Amazon partnership.

For Microsoft, the deal is a calculated retreat. Wedbush raised its price target to $575, arguing that the cap removes tail risk and locks in known IP rights. But the company is already hedging, acquiring AI startups to reduce its dependency on any single model provider. The era of the exclusive AI partnership, it seems, lasted barely three years.

**The floor: Salesforce and Anthropic**

At the other end of the AI economy, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff disclosed that his company is on track to spend $300 million on Anthropic tokens in 2026 — primarily for coding. The figure is remarkable not for its size but for what it replaces: Salesforce has effectively frozen software-engineer hiring, cut 4,000 support roles, and redirected the savings into AI model consumption.

Benioff’s framing was blunt. Internal AI tools, built on Anthropic’s Claude models, have boosted engineering productivity by 30 percent. Engineers who remain are transitioning into supervisory roles, managing autonomous coding agents rather than writing code themselves. The $300 million is not an experiment; it is an operating expense.

Anthropic’s own trajectory underscores the shift. The company’s enterprise revenue surged from roughly $1 billion in 2023 to $30 billion in 2025 — a growth rate that makes it, in revenue terms, the fastest-scaling enterprise software company in history.

**The Indian tech worker in the middle**

Both deals carry direct consequences for the Indian technology workforce. Microsoft’s Azure division employs tens of thousands of Indian-origin engineers, many of them on H-1B visas. If the company’s pivot toward acquiring smaller AI firms accelerates, the demand profile shifts from large-scale cloud-operations hiring to niche ML-research talent — a category where visa-holders face even fiercer competition.

Salesforce’s hiring freeze is more immediately painful. The company’s ecosystem — implementation partners, consultancies, managed-service providers — employs hundreds of thousands of workers in India through firms like Infosys, Wipro, and Cognizant. If Salesforce’s own engineers are being replaced by Claude, the downstream consultants who customise Salesforce deployments face the same logic with a shorter runway.

**What it means for India’s AI ambitions**

India’s government projects that AI could add up to $600 billion to the country’s GDP by 2035 — a figure cited in a recent NITI Aayog report. But the path to that number runs through exactly the kind of enterprise-AI adoption that Salesforce is demonstrating, which means fewer, not more, conventional engineering jobs.

The optimistic reading is that Indian engineers will move up the value chain: training models, fine-tuning them for local languages and regulatory contexts, and building the agentic workflows that sit on top of foundation models. The pessimistic reading is that the $300 million Salesforce is paying Anthropic is $300 million it is not paying Bengaluru.

Both readings are probably correct. The question is which one arrives first.
